description:
We are Sherket Moqawlat, and our vision is to transform the Visuals happening on Earth into Vocals, turning data into sound that people can feel. Sonify delivers the emotion behind the numbers, so the change happening to our planet becomes something you hear, connect with, and care about.

This is the mission we have taken upon ourselves:

"From Visuals to Vocals, feelings lead to action."
summary:
The Earth Science Jukebox challenge tasks teams with transforming complex Earth data into an auditory format. Sonify is our response to NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026’s Earth Science Jukebox challenge: an interactive web platform that transforms Earth Information Center datasets into soundscapes people can explore and hear. It will sonify global sea surface currents, annual temperature shifts, and sea-level changes, translating visual data patterns into harmonized audio through color mapping and sonification algorithms.
This approach bridges the gap between raw statistics and human emotion. By listening to the shifting climate, users experience the urgency of environmental changes directly. This methodology fulfills the challenge requirements by establishing a novel, accessible pathway for the public to engage with NASA data. It makes climate science inclusive and emotionally resonant.
details:
Sonify is an interactive web platform that turns NASA Earth science data into sound, so people can explore climate change by listening as well as viewing. It currently offers two experiences, A Warming Planet (annual global surface-temperature anomalies from NASA GISTEMP v4) and A Rising Ocean (global mean sea level from NASA GSFC Version 5.2), paired with visual context from NASA’s Earth Information Center.

Each year of data becomes one musical event. The chart, map and porthole display update to the same year as the sound. Users choose between two modes built from the same data. Science mode is for measurement. Pitch follows a linear scale (MIDI pitch = 62 + 8 × temperature in °C, or 62 + 2 × sea level in cm), a steady hum marks the zero reference, and a tick marks each change from the previous year, so listeners can judge both values and year-to-year differences by ear. Song mode is for engagement. Values map onto a 13-note pentatonic scale, loudness and brightness rise with the data, and the harmony moves through four chord stages as values increase. Users can play, pause, resume, seek, and change speed and volume.

Python processes the data (complete years only, with missing values never treated as zero). Tone.js and the Web Audio API generate the sound in real time in the browser. The audio clock is the single source of truth for playback, so the visuals stay aligned even when the user pauses or skips.

Benefits

Sonify adds a non-visual way to explore climate data for blind and low-vision users, who are often shut out by charts, maps and color. It also gives students, educators and the public an engaging way into NASA climate information. Because it is interactive, users can seek, replay and change speed, which fixed sonification videos do not allow. Every value is also available as text.

Intended impact

We want to close the access and interpretation gap in climate communication. Our slogan is “From Visuals to Vocals, we make people feel, so they can move.” Song mode helps people feel a trend, and Science mode lets them check the evidence. Sonify complements NASA’s visualizations rather than replacing them. We do not claim proven learning gains or guaranteed climate action, and we plan to test usability and comprehension.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python (data pipeline), JavaScript, Tone.js, the Web Audio API, Chrome and its developer tools, an automated test suite (18 tests run against the real datasets), GitHub, Vercel (hosting) and Canva (presentation and design). Claude and ChatGPT were used as AI assistants, with outputs reviewed by the team. Hardware was development laptops with headphones or speakers. Accessibility testing uses keyboard-only navigation and a screen reader such as NVDA or VoiceOver.

How it is creative

Sonify treats data as music instead of as a chart. Each year is a note, warmer years sound higher, and the harmony grows fuller and more restless as the planet changes. Sounds are matched to the topic: a cello-like melody and a heartbeat for warming, and glass bells, waves, a deep gliding voice and bubbles for rising seas. The two-mode design is also a creative choice. It separates faithful numerical mapping from musical expression instead of forcing one sound to do both jobs.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: our temperature series differs from NASA’s official average by no more than 0.018 °C since 1960. Audio output was measured in Chrome (the 1909 note measured 237 Hz against an expected value of about 235 Hz).
  • Honest mapping: higher values never produce lower notes, and missing data is never shown as zero.
  • Seasonal noise: using one note per year keeps long-term change audible.
  • Synchronization: sound and visuals follow one audio clock.
  • Accessibility: keyboard and screen-reader support, text alternatives, and audio that never starts unexpectedly.
  • Transparency: an explanation panel states the source, units, reference period, mapping and limitations.
